clue.text: Artist possibly producing proper art – Titian?

indicators.note: What is only possible is one of several ways things might fall out, so these letters are free to fall out in another order.

blocks.note: fifteen letters of fodder, the full width of the grid

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a piece of genuinely proper art might be a Titian.
explanation.walkthrough: Titian painted the Venetian nobility for a living, so the fodder names a man who did the job the answer describes. 'Possibly' looks like the setter marking a definition by example and is the shuffling instruction instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A portrait painter is an artist of one particular trade, the one who paints people, so 'artist' defines it by the wider class.

clue.text: Old leader revised Part 1 with support

indicators.note: To revise a thing is to go over it and set it down differently, so the letters come out arranged another way.

blocks.note: the word plus the Roman numeral for 1 makes five letters, reordered
an arch is what holds up a bridge or a doorway

explanation.surface: Someone has gone back over the opening section and propped it up.
explanation.walkthrough: The numeral is the easiest letter in the clue to read past, because '1' looks like a section number rather than an I. A patriarch leads a family, a tribe or an Orthodox church, never a country.
explanation.definitionFit: A patriarch is the old man at the head of a family or tribe, so age is built into the word rather than added by the clue.

clue.text: Staff carrying barrel over a round building

indicators.note: To carry a thing is to have it about you, inside a bag or a coat, so the letters named go within the word that carries them.
In a down clue what is over something is written above it, so the piece built first takes the top of the answer.

blocks.note: a rod is a staff, the stick carried as a badge of office
a tun is a large cask, the barrel wine and beer were stored in
the article taken straight from the clue

explanation.surface: A man with a staff lugging a barrel past a circular building.
explanation.walkthrough: TUN is the setter's favourite cask, a word that survives in 'tunnage' and almost nowhere else. The staff is split after two of its three letters, which is what stops the join showing.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotunda is a building or hall laid out on a circular plan, usually under a dome — the Pantheon in Rome being the model.

clue.text: Des, increasingly wan, turned up and fell ill again

indicators.note: In a down clue letters turned up are read from the foot of the space to the top, so both pieces arrive back to front.

blocks.note: growing more wan is growing paler, and the word arrives turned round
the man's name, turned round the same way

explanation.surface: Des, looking ever paler, showed up and then went down with it again.
explanation.walkthrough: Des is short for Desmond and is in the clue only for his three letters. What turns is the whole assembly rather than one piece of it, so the seam between name and adjective ends up buried in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To relapse is to fall back into an illness you had recovered from, so the past tense answers 'fell ill again' word for word.

clue.text: Publication is certain, though not right

indicators.note: 'Though not' withholds whatever it names, so that letter is struck out of the word just handed over.

blocks.note: the word taken straight from the clue
someone certain of a thing is sure of it
R is the standard abbreviation for right, and it is the letter dropped

explanation.surface: The magazine will definitely come out, though it is not the proper one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' does two jobs at once, holding the sentence together and handing over two letters of its own. Naming the letter to be lost rather than describing it is the fair way to set a deletion.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is one published number of a magazine or newspaper — the March issue — so the noun names a publication as it appears.

clue.text: Macho cider-making guy? One’s a fixer

blocks.note: cider is made by crushing apples in a press
a stud is a man who fancies himself irresistible
the noun the two descriptions hang on; 'macho' is the word supplying the letters

explanation.surface: A swaggering bloke who presses apples for a living.
explanation.walkthrough: English puts the describing word first, so a stud that presses is written the same way round as the clue's phrase — no instruction is needed to order the halves. 'Fixer' here fastens cloth rather than arranging deals.
explanation.definitionFit: A press stud is the little metal fastener that snaps two edges of fabric together, so it fixes them in the plainest sense of the word.

clue.text: I try an unusual way of receiving work?

indicators.note: What is unusual is not as it normally is, and letters called unusual are not in their normal order.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, exactly the length wanted

explanation.surface: Somebody describing an odd method of getting themselves hired.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder runs straight through the opening words, so the sentence has to be cut before 'unusual' rather than after it. 'Work' turns out to be the paperwork that lands on a desk, not employment.
explanation.definitionFit: An in-tray is the shallow desk tray incoming jobs are dropped into, so the definition names it by the office ritual it exists for.

clue.text: Rented property in outskirts of the French city

indicators.note: The outskirts of a town are its outer edges, so only the first and last letters of the word are taken.

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the three-letter word
Nancy is a city in Lorraine, in north-eastern France

explanation.surface: A rented flat out on the edge of a city in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' is the standard cue for LE or LA and is nothing of the kind here — the article belongs to the outskirts instruction and 'French' to the city. Nancy doubles as a girl's name, which is why setters keep her.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenancy is the holding of property under a lease, and by extension the property held, which is what renting gets you.

clue.text: Arrive at some rare achievement

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it and not the whole, so what is wanted is a run of letters already written inside the words.

blocks.note: the run starts on the third letter of the first word and stops two letters into the second

explanation.surface: Getting as far as something not many people manage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' stops looking like a quantity the moment you read it as a pointer at the words beside it. 'Arrive at' asks for a verb, which rules out the distance sense the surface keeps offering.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach a place is to arrive at it, and the verb stretches to reaching a total, an age or an agreement.

clue.text: Gossips time and time again engaged in lies

indicators.note: Something engaged in a thing is caught up inside it, so the letters named go within the word that follows.

blocks.note: tales told about people are lies
T is the standard abbreviation for time, and the clue asks for it twice

explanation.surface: Someone forever caught up in other people's untruths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time and time again' reads as an adverb meaning repeatedly and is really an instruction to write the abbreviation out twice. The pair goes in without disturbing a letter of what receives it.
explanation.definitionFit: To tattle is to pass on other people's business, so the third-person verb answers 'gossips' as an action rather than as the people doing it.

clue.text: European is not upset by a European country

indicators.note: Something upset has been knocked out of its arrangement, so these letters are to be put in another one.

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for European
five letters lifted straight off the page
the article makes the seventh letter

explanation.surface: A European claiming to be quite unbothered by one of the neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European' appears twice and does a different job each time, an abbreviation first and the definition's adjective second. The fodder sits on both sides of its own indicator, which is what makes it hard to gather up.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonia is the northernmost of the three Baltic states and an EU member since 2004, so 'European country' names it by its class.

clue.text: Pub, one with two names

blocks.note: one is the Roman numeral I
n. is the dictionary's short form of name, written out twice

explanation.surface: A pub called after a pair of people.
explanation.walkthrough: British pubs really are named after two things at once — the Fox and Hounds, the Eagle and Child — so the surface is telling the truth while the parse counts letters. Both abbreviations are the plainest kind there is.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn is a pub, particularly an old one with rooms upstairs, and the word is still carved over half the doorways in Britain.

clue.text: How NASA may activate rocket for publicity event?

blocks.note: you activate a control by pressing it
sending a rocket up is launching it
the American space agency sets the scene and hands over no letters

explanation.surface: The countdown business of getting an American rocket off the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves keep their space-programme senses and still add up to something out of the world of press releases, which is the whole joke. The question mark admits the countdown reading is the setter's invention rather than a phrase anyone uses.
explanation.definitionFit: A press launch is the event at which a company shows a new product to journalists, so 'publicity event' names it by its purpose.

clue.text: Settle area, moving houses etc.

definitions.note: Real estate is a mass noun covering land and whatever stands on it; 'houses etc.' names the contents in the plural, which is the shorthand an estate agent would use.

indicators.note: Things that are moving do not stay where they were put, and letters told to move end up somewhere else in the word.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, exactly the length wanted

explanation.surface: Populating a district by shifting people's homes about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settle' opens the clue looking like a verb with a job to do and is only fodder. 'Real' in the phrase is the lawyer's word for land, not the opposite of imaginary.
explanation.definitionFit: Real estate is property in land and buildings, so 'houses etc.' points at it through the most familiar thing it contains.

clue.text: Hitter hit out, being some way down the list?

indicators.note: To knock a thing out is to put it from its place, so the letters in front of the word do not stay in theirs.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, exactly the length wanted

explanation.surface: A batsman swinging wildly and finishing well down the rankings.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is two forms of the same verb, so the eye keeps trying to read a sentence where there is only a bag of letters. The question mark covers the fact that plenty of ordinals are 'some way down' and only the letters pin it to one.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirtieth marks the position of the thirtieth item in an order, far enough into any ranking to count as some way down it.

clue.text: Ancient story? I am surprised this is only half complete

indicators.note: Something only half complete stops at its midpoint, so the word beside it gives up its front two letters and no more.

blocks.note: 'My!' is the exclamation you make when startled
the front half of the four-letter word

explanation.surface: Astonishment that an old tale has only been told halfway through.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's 'this' points at nothing — it is a four-letter word waiting to be cut down the middle. 'My' as an exclamation is the one in 'my word' and 'oh my'.
explanation.definitionFit: A myth is a traditional tale out of the distant past, told to explain gods or beginnings, which is what 'ancient story' asks for.

clue.text: Hard American male plugging sweetheart for illicit cash

indicators.note: To plug a gap is to stop it up from inside, so the letter named goes into the middle of the word beside it.

blocks.note: H is the hardness grade stamped on a pencil
US is the standard short form for American
honey is what you call a sweetheart
M is the form-filler's abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A tough American man muscling in on somebody's girlfriend for dirty money.
explanation.walkthrough: Three abbreviations land in a row before the container even starts, and the male letter goes in after the sweetheart's first letter rather than into a tidy gap. 'Hard' is the pencil grade, not the man.
explanation.definitionFit: Hush money is what you pay someone to keep quiet about something, so the cash is illicit by definition rather than by circumstance.

clue.text: Popular salesman supporting public relations computer information

indicators.note: In a down clue what supports a thing is written underneath it, so these pieces go below the letters named next.

blocks.note: PR is the everyday short form of public relations
what is in is what is popular this season
a tout is the man selling tickets on the pavement outside the ground

explanation.surface: A well-liked rep working under the publicity department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting' is what does the stacking: in a down entry the supporters go at the foot, which sends the initials at the end of the clue to the top of the answer. A tout's tickets usually cost more than they are printed at.
explanation.definitionFit: A printout is the paper copy of what a computer is holding, so 'computer information' names it by what it carries off the screen.

clue.text: Dislike speed, avoiding start of sprint

indicators.note: To avoid a thing is to keep clear of it, so whatever it names is left out of the letters given.
The start of a word is the letter it begins with, so that one alone is taken.

blocks.note: haste is speed, as in 'more haste, less speed'
the opening letter of the word, and the one to be lost

explanation.surface: A loathing of going fast, and a habit of missing the gun.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words for speed share the clue, one to be cut up and one only to colour the sentence. The letter that goes is named by its position rather than spelt out, which is the fair way to set a deletion.
explanation.definitionFit: To hate something is to dislike it strongly, so the two verbs swap into a sentence without anything else changing.

clue.text: Not upset about relative in Somerset town

indicators.note: In a down clue letters upset are tipped over and read from the bottom up, so the word in front of it turns round.
To be about a thing is to lie round it, so the letters just turned close on either side of what comes next.

blocks.note: the three letters arrive the other way round
an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: Staying calm about a family member living down in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not upset' reads as one placid phrase and is really two instructions, the second acting on the first. The relative goes in whole and unaltered, which is rare enough to be worth spotting.
explanation.definitionFit: Taunton is the county town of Somerset in south-west England, known for its cider and its cricket ground, so the definition places it by county.

clue.text: Sentence hurts the head of silly people

blocks.note: bird is British slang for a spell in prison — 'doing bird'
to brain somebody is to hit them over the head

explanation.surface: A prison term that gives foolish people a headache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' for a stretch inside comes from rhyming slang — birdlime for time — and is still what British prisoners call it. 'Head of' sits there looking like an instruction to take a first letter and is nothing of the sort.
explanation.definitionFit: A birdbrain has no more brain than a bird has, so the plural names a set of fools by the insult rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Suggested mischievous character didn’t tell the truth

blocks.note: an imp is a small mischievous sprite
someone who did not tell the truth lied

explanation.surface: A little troublemaker caught out in a fib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' invites you to hunt for a single letter and wants a creature instead, which is the only obstacle here — the two pieces then simply meet, with nothing hidden or turned. 'Suggested' is the courtroom sense: said without being said.
explanation.definitionFit: To imply something is to suggest it without stating it outright, and both words are past tenses, so the swap is clean.

clue.text: Meeting for which some visitors are late?

definitions.text: Meeting for which some visitors are late?

blocks.note: the surface offers an ordinary gathering with a start time and a few stragglers
the other sense of late is dead, and guests who answer to that have come a long way

explanation.surface: A meeting at which a few of those invited fail to turn up on time.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the only warning that 'late' has swapped meanings. Read it as the obituary column does and the sentence turns over: the visitors are not delayed, they are departed.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight once 'late' means deceased — the gathering exists precisely in order to receive guests who are dead.

clue.text: Educational payment? End with total NUS disputed

indicators.note: What is disputed is not accepted as it stands, so these letters need not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: three letters of fodder
eight more, NUS being the National Union of Students, the body that speaks for students in Britain

explanation.surface: The students' union arguing over a final figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Fodder broken across a link word is easy to under-collect: the sum wanted runs from the first word to the last before the indicator. A set of initials makes unusually convenient fodder because it carries no meaning to distract you.
explanation.definitionFit: A student loan is the money a British undergraduate borrows for fees and living costs, so it is the payment education runs on.

clue.text: Mild dispute about river fish

indicators.note: To be about a thing is to lie round it, so the word in front closes on both sides of the letter named.

blocks.note: a spat is a small quarrel
R is the map-maker's abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A minor row over a stretch of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning' and works as 'surrounding', which is the pivot the clue turns on. Spat is the pettiest word English has for a quarrel, which is why 'mild' is doing no work beyond confirming it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprat is a small sea fish of the herring family, eaten whole and smoked, and the one setters reach for when five letters are wanted.

clue.text: Europe rather suppressing this stage work

indicators.note: To suppress a thing is to hold it down out of sight, so what is wanted lies buried unbroken in the words in front.

blocks.note: the run starts on the third letter of the first word and stops two letters into the second

explanation.surface: Europe keeping the lid on a piece of theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rather' is there to bridge the two words the letters run across, so reading it as an adverb of degree loses the join. A stage work of this kind is sung the whole way through, which is what separates it from a play.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera is a drama set to music and sung on stage, so 'stage work' names it by where it happens and what it is.

clue.text: Expat in part of Melbourne, primarily

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes first, so each of the words gives up its opening letter and nothing more.

blocks.note: the first letter of the first word
the little word counts as one of the three and gives up its O
the city's initial finishes the run

explanation.surface: A British emigrant living in one particular corner of Melbourne.
explanation.walkthrough: The instruction sits at the very end, so the phrase in front reads as a district until you reach it. Melbourne is in the clue for more than its letter: it is Australians who use the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Pom is the Australian nickname for a British immigrant — as in 'whingeing pom' — so an expat Briton down under is one.

clue.text: Regret pinching English money for followers

indicators.note: To pinch a thing is to take hold of it and keep it, so those letters end up gripped inside the word that pinches them.

blocks.note: to rue something is to regret it
E is the standard abbreviation for English
tin is old slang for money, of the same vintage as brass

explanation.surface: Regret at the pocketing of English cash by the hangers-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' reads as stealing and works as enclosing, and the two senses share the same grip. Two pieces go in together rather than one, splitting the short word after its opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the train of attendants who travel with an important person, so 'followers' names them by what they spend the day doing.

clue.text: Book recalled in embracing love and passion

indicators.note: Something recalled is called back the way it came, so those letters are read from the last to the first.
To embrace a thing is to put your arms round it, so the word named closes on both sides of what follows.

blocks.note: a tome is a weighty book, and it arrives turned round
the word taken straight from the clue
love is a tennis score of nothing, written as a nought

explanation.surface: A book called back in for dwelling on romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is not doing its usual job as a preposition — it hands over both letters and then opens up to take the tennis nought. 'Recalled' is a manufacturer's recall on the surface and a turnaround in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotion is a strong feeling, and passion is the commonest name for one, so the two nouns stand in for each other.

clue.text: The trendy dealer, not well treated with kindness

indicators.note: Someone not well is out of sorts, and letters in that state are not in the order they ought to be.

blocks.note: fifteen letters of fodder, the full width of the grid

explanation.surface: A fashionable trader who is off colour being looked after gently.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma marks where the fodder stops, and the phrase after it reads as sympathy while working as an instruction. A fifteen-letter anagram looks forbidding and is the friendliest kind, because the crossings pin it down fast.
explanation.definitionFit: To act tender-heartedly is to act with a soft heart, which is what doing a thing with kindness amounts to.
